source: Lovett & Anderson (1995) Making heads or tails out of selecting problem-solving strategies (CogSci proceedings; companion of the 1996 JEP:LMC paper)
finding: Building Sticks Task: each problem can be started by undershoot or overshoot. Solvers learned each strategy's success rate and chose the more successful one more often, at group level close to probability matching. Many individuals overmatched.
numbers: N=67 after 1 exclusion (68 run). 90 problems. Four conditions: complementary or not x 80/20 or 60/40. Matching-law equilibrium for MS-first: about .94 (noncomp-hi), .69 (noncomp-lo); observed fit. Extreme users (MS on >=43 of last 45): 3 of comp-hi (18%), 2 of noncomp-lo (13%), 1 of comp-lo (6%). Individual fit to matching law R2=.60.
limits: Group matching hides individual exclusive users. Per-condition N not reported (about 15-17). Artificial two-strategy task; strategies fixed and known to the solver.
agent_relevance: Strategy choice can be a cheap learned success-rate estimate per strategy per problem class. A router should keep counts of successes and failures per strategy per class and pick the best, with some noise for exploration (G12).

source: Lovett & Anderson (1995) ACT-R account of strategy selection in the Building Sticks Task
finding: ACT-R model: each strategy is a production with a Bayesian estimate of its probability of success from past successes and failures; the highest noisy estimate wins. One free parameter (alpha+beta=255, noise variance .052).
numbers: R2=.99 for binned group data (all problems); R2=.66 for individual subjects' last 45 problems. Predicts preference grows with the success difference and weakens when strategies are similar.
limits: Large individual variance unexplained (about 34% in individuals). Authors suggest differences in learning rate and exploration-exploitation balance.
agent_relevance: Gives a minimal formal selection rule (Beta posterior plus noise) that code can run. It is a counted statistic, not model judgment, so it fits G5.

source: Schunn, Lovett & Reder (2001) Awareness and working memory in strategy adaptivity. Memory & Cognition 29(2):254-266
finding: Same BST with success base rates that shift mid-task. People differ in how far they shift strategy use. Those who explicitly noticed the shift adapted much more. Working memory capacity did not predict adaptivity.
numbers: Exp 1: N=56. Aware of shift N=18, unaware N=37. Block 4 to 7 shift in overshoot use: .44 aware vs .17 unaware, F(1,53)=12.7, p<.001. Observed adaptivity distribution flatter than chance (chi2(3)=13.0, p<.01; 20% had zero or less adaptivity vs 9% expected). Exp 3: dual-task load did not change adaptivity.
limits: Awareness measured by debriefing after the fact in Exp 1 (correlational). Challenges purely implicit models (ACT-R, SSL) and pure working-memory accounts. Exp 2-3 details read in outline only.
agent_relevance: Strategy change works better when the shift is made explicit. In our agent the S6 impasse detector plus a code-kept success table is the explicit notice. Do not rely on the model to feel that a strategy stopped working (G1, G10).

source: Frontiers in Psychology (2025) Task representation and individual differences affect strategy selection and problem-solving performance (Building Sticks Task; tests RCCL of Lovett & Schunn 1999)
finding: Tests RCCL (Represent-Construct-Choose-Learn): people build strategies from the current task representation, choose by estimated success, learn rates, and re-represent the task when all strategies do poorly. Base rates were learned, cues were partly dropped, and representation changed more under low success.
numbers: N=100 analysed of 144 recruited (44 excluded). 80 training problems. Cue sensitivity b=1.03, z=3.52, p<.001. Bias x time b=.39, p=.03; posttest biased group chose the high-base-rate strategy more (b=.46, p=.009). Cue dropping incomplete in unpredictive-biased condition (slope b=.49). Self-reported length-based use 45% (unpredictive) vs 69% (predictive), chi2=10.79. Representation change .71 vs .58, F(1,98)=8.09, p=.005. Inductive reasoning and attentional control predicted faster solving; working memory did not.
limits: The paper does NOT replicate Lovett & Anderson 1996; it tests RCCL. The representation-change effect may come mainly from the unpredictive factor (interaction not significant). One task family. Last 23,767 characters of the page not read.
agent_relevance: A rule for the agent: when every strategy in the repertoire fails, change the representation (S2) rather than retry the same strategies. Links to the representational-change subfield (parallel).

source: Siegler (1996, 2006) overlapping waves theory, as stated in Fazio, DeWolf & Siegler (2016)
finding: Core claims: at any time a person knows several strategies; the same person uses different ones on similar problems and even on the same problem twice. Choice is adaptive to speed and accuracy. Improvement comes from four changes: discovering new strategies, relying more on efficient ones, choosing more adaptively, and executing better.
numbers: Theory statement, no single number. Applied before to arithmetic, reading, spelling, motor skills, infant-mother interaction and tool use.
quote: At any given time, a person knows multiple ways of solving a problem. The strategy that is chosen depends on characteristics of both the problem and the learner.
limits: A later restatement, not Siegler's own book. Original data (Siegler & Jenkins 1989; Emerging Minds 1996) not opened.
agent_relevance: Hold a repertoire, not one method, and pick per problem. Variability is normal; but under G4 several strategy-voters on one answer are still not independent.

source: Fazio, DeWolf & Siegler (2016) Strategy use and strategy choice in fraction magnitude comparison. JEP:LMC 42(1):1-16
finding: Adults with strong maths used many strategies tailored to the problem type. Weaker students used flawed strategies and, when shown a correct alternative, rarely switched to it. Bad strategy use came from lack of understanding of what makes a strategy valid, not from failing to think of options.
numbers: Exp 1: N=19 selective-university students, 48 problems, 19 distinct strategies identified, mean 11.21 (SD 1.9) per person, range 6 to 15; 96% correct; logical-necessity strategies 26% of trials, intermediate-step 51%, usually-correct 16%, questionable 7%. Guessing was right on 79% of trials. Exp 2: N=19 community-college students, 74% correct overall (10 students about 93%, 9 students about 52%). Coding agreement 90%.
limits: Small N; one domain (fractions); strategies coded from self-report. Exp 3 read only in outline.
agent_relevance: A longer strategy list does not help unless the agent can check why a strategy is valid. Selection needs an applicability check (S0 gate, G3), not only recall of options.

source: Fazio, DeWolf & Siegler (2016) Experiment 3: choosing among own, correct and incorrect strategy
finding: Students were shown three strategies for a problem (their own, a correct alternative, an incorrect one). They mostly kept their own. Weaker students rarely moved from a wrong strategy to a right one.
numbers: Kept original strategy on 57% of trials (SD 20). Switches went to the correct alternative more often than to a wrong one, t(25)=5.23, p<.001, d=1.06 (one mean reported as 9%, SD 11). High and low group contrasts only partly extracted.
limits: Detailed split between high and low performers not fully verified in this read.
agent_relevance: Showing alternatives after an agent has committed may not change its approach; choose the strategy before commitment (S0/S2).

source: Gick & Holyoak (1980) Analogical problem solving. Cognitive Psychology 12:306-355, Experiments I-II (Duncker radiation problem)
finding: Subjects who read a military story with a dispersion solution and were told to use it as a hint solved Duncker's radiation problem far more often than controls. A story whose problem statement resembled the radiation problem transferred better than a disanalogous one.
numbers: Exp I: N=40 (10 per cell). Dispersion solution: 100% after Attack-Dispersion story vs 0% control. Exp II: N=143. Complete+partial dispersion: 76% attack story (N=47), 49% parade story (N=45), 8% control (N=50); complete only 57%, 31%, 8%.
limits: Hint was explicit. Text read from a slide-hosted copy, not the journal PDF.
agent_relevance: Analogy is strong when the source is supplied and flagged, so an analogy operator needs a step that supplies the source (see a09). Rewriting the new problem in abstract terms before retrieval should raise match rate.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1980) Experiments III-V: spontaneous noticing of the analogy
finding: Without a hint, most subjects did not notice that the stored story applied. Once told, they could use it. The bottleneck is noticing, not applying. Self-generated military solutions gave a partial boost.
numbers: Exp III N=45: 41% (9 of 22) radiation dispersion solutions after generating a military dispersion solution vs 13% (3 of 23) without. Exp IV N=27: hint 92% (11 of 12) vs no hint 20% (3 of 15); 12 of 15 no-hint subjects said it did not occur to them. Exp V N=47: 10% before story; Story First 41% no hint, 76% overall after hint; incubation control 10%.
quote: The main obstacle to using an analogy is failing to notice that it applies to the target problem.
limits: The story was learned in a recall task, a possible source of distance. The often quoted '10% spontaneous, 92% with hint' mixes the Exp V baseline with the Exp IV hint figure.
agent_relevance: The strategy gap is recall at the right time. A code gate that asks 'which solved problem is this like' would close it; do not trust the model to notice unprompted. Tests our S1 restatement step.

source: Behrens (2003) Thinking outside of the box: on Karl Duncker and functional fixedness. Gestalt Theory 25(1/2) (secondary account of Duncker 1945)
finding: Duncker's box problem (later called the candle problem): when the boxes already held tacks, matches and candles, solving was harder than when they were empty. Duncker said the habitual function narrows attention and a switch he called recentering is needed. His problems: gimlet, box, pliers, weight, paperclip, and radiation.
numbers: No Duncker numbers in this source; it says fixedness may require twice as long to solve.
quote: he concluded that our preconceptions of a thing's function so clouds and restricts our attention
limits: Secondary source. The 1945 monograph was not opened.
agent_relevance: A Duncker-style re-description of tools or objects is a documented escape from fixation. Link to Anomaly handling and fixation (parallel).

source: Duncker (1945) On problem-solving. Psychological Monographs 58(5) (translated by L. S. Lees from the 1935 German book)
finding: Bibliographic record only (112 pages). Founding text of the view that solving proceeds by successive narrowing from a general solution through a functional solution to a specific one.
numbers: Not read. No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened; the general-to-functional-to-specific chain is background knowledge, unverified here.
agent_relevance: Treat as unread. A later pass should obtain the monograph and record the exact radiation-problem protocol results.

source: Simon (1973) The structure of ill-structured problems. Artificial Intelligence 4:181-201
finding: Search listing only: the line between well- and ill-structured problems is blurry, the same information-processing principles apply to both, and ill-structured problems are worked on by splitting off well-structured parts. Reed (2016) later supported this.
numbers: Not read. Six well-structuredness criteria cited by a secondary source; only two confirmed (a definite test for a solution; a problem space with states).
limits: Download failed; not opened. Reed (2016) not opened.
agent_relevance: Our S0 gate can follow Simon: if no checker exists, first turn the problem into a sub-problem that has one.

source: Dörner & Funke (2017) Complex problem solving: what it is and what it is not. Frontiers in Psychology 8:1153
finding: Reviews Lohhausen and MicroDYN. Lohhausen: a simulated town with over 2000 variables run as mayor for 10 years compressed into 10 hours. Success was not predicted by IQ but by staying calm and switching between analytic and holistic modes. Argues MicroDYN is too simple because one strategy (VOTAT) is enough.
numbers: Lohhausen over 2000 variables, 10 simulated years in 10 hours, student participants (N not stated in the text read). Jansson (1994) lists seven failure areas. MicroDYN: 3 to 5 variables, 3 minutes to explore. Quote from Funke (2014b): 'Minimal complex systems run the danger of becoming minimal valid systems.' First 100,000 of 148,000 characters read in detail; the remainder was references.
limits: Read through a page fetcher, so wording is partly the tool's summary. No correlation coefficients given. Lohhausen N and IQ figures come from Dörner et al. 1983, not opened.
agent_relevance: The failure list (act on current feedback only, thematic vagabonding, selective information, no self-reflection, hasty action, global hypotheses, fewer tests) is a test list for trace review (S9). It also matches G1 and G2.

source: Dörner & Funke (2017): the emergency reaction under complexity and generic error lists
finding: Dörner's 'emergency reaction': reduced intellectual level (less self-reflection, fewer intentions, more stereotyping), hasty action (more risk, more rule violations, escape), and degraded hypothesis work (more global hypotheses, fewer tests, entrenchment). Ramnarayan et al. (1997) generic errors: inadequate plans, learning blocked by stereotype knowledge, reactive instead of proactive action.
numbers: No numbers; qualitative lists.
limits: Human behavior under stress; LLMs have no stress, so the match is by pattern only.
agent_relevance: Map to LLM failures: reactive patching, shallow hypotheses, entrenchment on the first plan. Candidate code checks for trace audits.

source: Funke (2015) Complex problem solving: single ability or complex phenomenon? Frontiers in Psychology 6:1669 (opinion)
finding: Five features of a complex problem: complexity, interrelatedness, intransparency, dynamics, polytely. MicroDYN meets few: up to three inputs and outputs, mostly no side effects, no conflicting goals, a short four-step solution phase. It mainly tests interactive hypothesis testing and the control-of-variables strategy.
numbers: MicroDYN-CPS accounts for about 5% variance in school grades beyond fluid intelligence (modal result). Items with eigendynamics: none in Greiff & Funke 2010; 64% (Study 1) and 42% (Study 2) in Greiff et al. 2012.
limits: Opinion paper with a critical stance; the 5% figure summarizes modal results, not one study.
agent_relevance: Benchmarks for the agent should not rely on MicroDYN-like toy systems alone; hidden interactions and conflicting goals are where strategy failures show.

source: Funke (2014) Analysis of minimal complex systems and complex problem solving require different forms of causal cognition. Frontiers in Psychology 5:739
finding: Minimal complex systems (MicroDYN) can be fully analysed in about 3 minutes by varying one input at a time (VOTAT, Tschirgi 1980). Knowledge-rich systems (Tailorshop, 12 simulated months; MORO, 20 years) have too many variables for that, so people use assumed causal relations, global monitoring and heuristics.
numbers: Time frames only: about 3 minutes for full analysis; items designed for about 5 minutes. No percentages.
limits: Conceptual argument, no new data.
agent_relevance: VOTAT is a complete, checkable strategy for small hidden systems. A probing operator that changes one input and records the output fits when the system is small.

source: Stadler, Becker, Gödker, Leutner & Greiff (2015) Complex problem solving and intelligence: a meta-analysis. Intelligence 53:92-101
finding: CPS and intelligence correlate substantially. How CPS is measured moderates it; the newest approaches (MicroDYN type) correlate most.
numbers: 47 studies, 60 independent samples, total N=13,740. Mean effect size g=.433.
limits: Only the abstract was seen through search results; full text restricted.
agent_relevance: CPS overlaps general ability about as much as fluid-ability tests do, so a strategy router cannot replace a stronger model.

source: Süß (1999) critique of complex problem solving as a general ability, reported in a German source
finding: Reported in a search result: across a large study, performance on different complex problems correlated weakly, and correlations nearly vanished after controlling for processing capacity and domain prior knowledge.
numbers: No figures seen.
limits: Not opened; secondhand statement only.
agent_relevance: A general problem-solving skill may be mostly knowledge plus capacity. Measure gain per problem class, not a general skill (G7).

source: Rieskamp & Otto (2006) SSL: a theory of how people learn to select strategies. JEP:General 135(2):207-236, as reanalyzed in Rieskamp (2008) Judgment and Decision Making 3(3)
finding: SSL is reinforcement learning over strategies: the chance of choosing a strategy is its expectancy divided by the sum of expectancies; expectancy rises by the payoff when the strategy was chosen; parameters set initial preference, learning rate and application error. Classifying people by end-of-study behavior mislabels them because they learn.
numbers: Study 1 reanalysis N=24: w=18, beta_TTB=.41, error=.18, mean predicted choice probability .71 (SD .05). Study 2 reanalysis N=120: w=36, error=.26, predicted probability .58 vs .33 chance. After a switch to a compensatory environment only 27% moved to a compensatory strategy; after a switch to a noncompensatory one, 65% moved to take-the-best. The forgetting extension (phi=.07) was preferred for 30 of 120 by AIC.
quote: Strategies that performed better gained selection share, and initial preferences were overridden by experience.
limits: Secondary reanalysis, not the 2006 paper (full text not found). Tasks are cue-based inference strategies, not full problem solving.
agent_relevance: A ready formal selector: expectancy per strategy, updated by realized payoff. It predicts entrenchment (strong early preferences slow adaptation). Add a forgetting factor to our strategy table (G12).

source: Shrager & Siegler (1998) SCADS: a model of children's strategy choices and strategy discoveries. Psychological Science 9:405-410
finding: Abstract and secondary summaries: strategies are sequences of simple operators; new ones are generated by heuristics (such as dropping redundant steps) and filtered by metacognitive constraints (such as both addends must be represented). The model matched children's addition data in at least eight ways, including adaptive choice and the order of discovery.
numbers: No figures read. A later multiplication study found SCADS could not form all children's multiplication strategies from recombined addition operators.
limits: Not opened; description from search snippets.
agent_relevance: A discover-then-filter loop is a model for letting the agent compose new strategies from atomic operators (O1-O8) with code-checked legality constraints instead of free generation.

source: Luwel, Torbeyns, Schillemans & Verschaffel (2009) Priming effects in strategy choice, seen from Siegler's strategic change theory. Pedagogische Studien 86:369-384 (Dutch)
finding: Reviews overlapping waves and SCADS, including its priming module, and tests the prediction that a recently used strategy is chosen again. Two experiments on grid-counting tasks confirmed it.
numbers: Exp 1: subtraction strategy used .45 after subtraction primes vs .41 after addition primes; F(1,30)=5.68, p=.02, partial eta2=.16; the effect appeared only at 31 blocks (d=.16, p<.01). Primes elicited the target strategy on 99.88% of trials (3 of 2,557 failed). Exp 2 gave a similar effect (F(1,23)=16.32, p<.001).
limits: Small effect; adults; counting task; read in outline (Dutch).
agent_relevance: Recent strategy use biases choice. In long agent runs an earlier operator can bias later ones; reset the repertoire state at problem boundaries.

source: Luchins (1942) Mechanization in problem solving: the effect of Einstellung. Psychological Monographs 54(6)
finding: From search summaries only: after six problems solvable by one long method, most people used it on critical problems that had a shorter one. A direct instruction ('Don't be blind') helped over half. An unprimed control group found the short method at once.
numbers: A garbled OCR snippet suggests about 77% Einstellung solutions on the first two critical problems in one freshman sample; not verified.
limits: PDF download failed; figures unverified.
agent_relevance: Persistence on a past method follows from any success-count selector. A code-side check ('is a simpler route available') after a long success run is the matching guard.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: large language models self-compose reasoning structures (arXiv 2402.03620)
finding: Stage 1 (once per task): three meta-prompts SELECT relevant atomic reasoning modules, ADAPT them and IMPLEMENT a JSON reasoning structure. Stage 2 (each instance): follow the structure. Beats CoT and Plan-and-Solve.
numbers: BBH average: PaLM 2-L direct 56%, CoT 60%, Plan-and-Solve 61%, Self-Discover 67%; GPT-4 58, 75, 73, 81. T4D: PaLM 2-L 30/40/42/69; GPT-4 51/52/53/85. MATH (200 sampled): PaLM 2-L 45/42/49/50.5; GPT-4 70.5/71/70/73. Beats direct on 23/25 and CoT on 21/25 tasks (PaLM 2-L). 10-40x fewer inference calls than CoT-self-consistency. 74.7% of MATH failures were calculation errors.
limits: Structures learned from a few unlabeled task examples; gains largest on world-knowledge tasks, small on MATH. The model chooses the modules (G5 risk).
agent_relevance: Closest published analog to our S0/S2 strategy routing. Per-task selection costs about 3 extra calls. Keep the selection step but add a code check and compare at equal tokens (G7).

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-most prompting enables complex reasoning (arXiv 2205.10625)
finding: Decomposition strategy: break the problem into easier subproblems, then solve them in order, feeding earlier answers forward. Large gains on length generalization, small on GSM8K.
numbers: SCAN length split: at least 99% with 14 exemplars vs 16% for chain-of-thought. Last-letter concatenation at length 12: CoT 37.4% (4 exemplars), 38.4% (8). GSM8K: CoT 60.97% to least-to-most 62.39%; for problems needing 5+ steps 39.07% to 45.23%.
limits: Exemplars are task specific and the SCAN decomposition prompts are hand written.
agent_relevance: Decomposition pays when the problem is longer than the examples; near neutral on short problems. Supports routing: use decomposition only when the step count is high (G11, G12).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (arXiv 2310.01714; ICLR 2024)
finding: Analogy strategy: the model recalls relevant problems itself and then solves the new one, with no hand-written exemplars. Beats 0-shot and often few-shot CoT.
numbers: GSM8K: 5-shot CoT with GPT-3.5-turbo 75.0%, self-generated exemplars 75.8% to 77.8% across variants. MATH GPT-3.5-turbo: 33.0 to 33.9-37.3. BIG-Bench word sorting 3-shot CoT 67.6% vs 68.4%; temporal sequences 44.8% vs 58.0%. Codeforces: GPT-3.5-turbo 15% Acc@1 with self-generated knowledge+exemplars vs GPT-4 16%.
limits: Table 1 columns were hard to align in the text extraction, so only stable rows are quoted. Gains small on easy tasks.
agent_relevance: Analogy as an operator needs recalled solved problems; self-generated ones are noisy but cheap. Recall is the Gick-Holyoak bottleneck (a09); here a prompt forces it.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve prompting (arXiv 2305.04091)
finding: Plan first, then execute. PS+ adds detailed instructions against calculation errors. An error analysis of zero-shot CoT found three failure types.
numbers: Error analysis of 46 wrong GSM8K answers from zero-shot CoT (GPT-3): calculation 7%, missing step 12%, semantic misunderstanding 27%. Zero-shot averages over six arithmetic sets (text-davinci-003): CoT 70.4, PoT 73.5, PS 72.9, PS+ 76.7; few-shot manual CoT 77.6. PS+ on GSM8K 59.3.
limits: Small error sample; shares do not sum to 100% (rest unclassified); PoT/PS row order reconstructed from a text table.
agent_relevance: Planning prompts are cheap, but semantic misunderstanding is the largest error class and a plan does not fix it; a restate step (S1) targets it.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a step back: evoking reasoning via abstraction in LLMs (arXiv 2310.06117)
finding: Abstraction strategy: first ask for the high-level concept or principle, then reason from it. Large gains on knowledge-heavy tasks.
numbers: PaLM-2L: MMLU Physics 66.4% to 73.2%, Chemistry 70.9% to 81.8%; TimeQA 41.5% to 66%; MuSiQue +7%. CoT alone: 65% Physics, 75.3% Chemistry. MMLU Physics error analysis: fixes 20.5% of baseline errors, introduces 11.9% new ones; over 90% of remaining errors are reasoning or math errors.
limits: Mostly one model family (PaLM-2L, GPT-4 in some rows). Benefit depends on retrieving the right principle.
agent_relevance: Abstraction fits knowledge tasks; do not use it as a default. It is one router class: use when the question hangs on a named principle.

source: Adaptive-Solver (arXiv 2310.01446, 2023) Dynamic strategy selection in LLM reasoning
finding: After each attempt a consistency check (3 samples, threshold 1) decides whether to adapt: change model, prompting method, or decomposition granularity. Escalation goes from simple to more specialized methods.
numbers: Arithmetic average: best fixed baseline (CoT-SC) 85.8%; AS-P 87.2, AS-D 87.8, AS-PD 88.6. Model adaptation from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 matched GPT-4 alone and saved 35.8% to 53.6% cost (GSM8K 93.5 vs 93.0, 48.3% saved; CSQA 82.0 vs 85.5). Average solving rounds 1.20 (AS-P), 1.38 (AS-D), 1.44 (AS-PD).
limits: Backbone GPT-3.5-turbo-0301; 200 samples per dataset for model-adaptation runs. The signal is agreement between samples of one model, which G4 says is not independent proof. Last 14,547 characters not read.
agent_relevance: Matches our G1/G12 design: switch strategy only when a signal fails, simple first. Replace the weak agreement signal with a held-out check where one exists.

source: Meta-Reasoner (arXiv 2502.19918v4) Dynamic guidance for optimized inference-time reasoning in LLMs
finding: A contextual bandit (LinUCB) reads a short progress report after each reasoning step and picks the next high-level strategy: continue, restart, backtrack, decompose. A dynamic version lets the model propose new strategies as new arms.
numbers: Game of 24 (GPT-4o-mini): CoT 4%, ToT 65%, MACM 80%, Meta-Reasoner 89% (92% with GPT-4o). Bandit removed: 82%; no progress report: 85%. Fixed arms K=3: 65%, K=5: 72%, dynamic: 89%. TheoremQA: CoT 39.46%, Reflexion 74.32%, Meta-Reasoner 84.13%.
limits: Bandit tuned on 30-50 queries per task; single runs, no variance; same model generates and scores the reward; mixed backbones; training range overlaps test range for Game of 24.
agent_relevance: Shows bandit-over-strategies is feasible, but the reward is self-scored (G5, G10 risk). Use code-computed rewards (checks passed) and per-class counts.

source: Synthesis (analyst) of three formal strategy selectors: ACT-R success estimate, SSL expectancy, SCADS distribution-with-discovery (from a02, a19, a20, a04)
finding: Three formal selectors exist: ACT-R Bayesian success estimate with noise (Lovett & Anderson), SSL expectancy-proportional reinforcement (Rieskamp & Otto), and SCADS distribution with discovery (Shrager & Siegler). All pick from a known repertoire by learned success. None, in the sources read, models first choice from problem features without feedback.
numbers: Fits already recorded: ACT-R R2=.99 group, .66 individual; SSL predicted probability .71 (N=24) and .58 (N=120) vs chance .33.
limits: Analyst synthesis of lines already recorded, not a new source; the claim about feature-based first choice is a reading and needs checking against Siegler's ASCM (Siegler & Shipley 1995, not opened).
agent_relevance: Cold start: the first problem of a class has no success history. Use a prior set by task class at the S0 gate, then update from counted checks.

source: Dörner, Kreuzig, Reither & Stäudel (1983) Lohhausen, and Dörner (1996) The Logic of Failure, via secondary snippets
finding: Secondary: participants who handled the town badly fell into stress and erratic behavior, with much talk and little sensible action; good participants made more decisions, asked more why-questions and reflected on their own behavior (the last point reported for the related Greenvale scenario).
numbers: No N or coefficients obtained. The Lexikon page returned 403.
limits: Not opened; snippets only. The Greenvale detail comes from a blog post, not Lohhausen itself.
agent_relevance: A lead only. The good solver's signature (why-questions plus self-reflection) is a testable trace feature for our agent.

source: Kotovsky, Hayes & Simon (1985) Why are some problems hard? Evidence from Tower of Hanoi. Cognitive Psychology 17:248-294
finding: Bibliographic only: Tower of Hanoi isomorphs with different rules and move formats were solved at very different speeds, so representation and rule difficulty, not problem-space size alone, drive difficulty.
numbers: Not read; no figures. Search did not confirm any 'monster move' or '16 times' claim.
limits: Citation confirmed from a CV; findings are background knowledge.
agent_relevance: Isomorphic problems differ in difficulty by representation. Supports a normalize step (S2) before strategy choice.
